The Pentagon ’s chief strategist walked out of a Nato meeting in Brussels after rebuking Ukraine over its long-range strikes inside Russia , according to a report .
The Telegraph reported that Elbridge Colby, the US under secretary of defence for policy, told the Ukrainian Defence Contact Group (UDCG) on Tuesday that Kyiv’s deep-strike campaign lacked military value and had failed to blunt Russian advances on the front line.
Mr Colby reportedly walked out of the room immediately after delivering his remarks, departing before Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara could present a classified battlefield briefing.
The incident has sparked concerns regarding Washington’s stance toward Ukraine, with German sources telling the newspaper that Mr Colby’s behaviour suggests that the Trump administration has, in effect, sided with the Kremlin against Europe.
The rebuke follows an intensified campaign of long-range strikes targeting Russian arms factories and oil infrastructure, where Ukrainian drones and missiles have struck 28 major Russian oil refineries in more than 200 confirmed attacks this year.
Mr Colby’s remarks have prompted sharp pushback from British and European ministers, who view strikes on Russian oil refineries and weapons factories – alongside this week’s Ukrainian raid that collapsed a section of the Kerch Bridge – as vital in weakening Vladimir Putin’s war effort.
Defence secretary Wes Streeting defended Kyiv’s strategy following Tuesday’s talks, stating that the strikes “helped to degrade Putin’s war machine, buying time and saving lives,” while German defence minister Boris Pistorius dismissed Mr Colby’s assessment as “stupid”.
German officials also pointed to the perceived contradiction in Washington’s stance given the US military’s own reliance on long-range strikes in its campaign against Iran .
A second source confirmed Mr Colby left as soon as media departed, leaving US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker to represent Washington for the remainder of the session.
Mr Colby subsequently addressed reporters in the atrium of Nato headquarters at around 5pm local time before departing for the airport to catch a flight.
The diplomatic friction comes ahead of a major summit of the “coalition of the willing” in Berlin on Thursday, which prime minister Andy Burnham will co-chair alongside his French and German counterparts.
Around 40 leaders – joined by Donald Trump’s peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – are due to discuss long-term security guarantees and post-war reconstruction plans for Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
“It’s not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up,” Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The “peace declaration” released after the meeting made no mention of Russia’s war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market on Nov. 19, 2026: Dow drops 1,100 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq end sharply lower as Anthropic sees huge pop in trading debut
articles.title_zh: Stock Market on Nov. 19, 2026: Dow drops 1,100 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq end sharply lower as Anthropic sees huge pop in trading debut
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.
Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.
"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.
Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.
San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.
Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.
Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.
The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to investment bank Renaissance Capital, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k) , given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.
Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.
However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.
Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.
AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms . Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans . The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.
As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict live
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya community
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Rohingya refugees were seen reacting as the ICJ verdict was broadcast on a big screen in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.
They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attachÃ© be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

articles.title_orig: Trump eyes 2027 to 'see what happens' with Iran
articles.title_zh: Trump eyes 2027 to 'see what happens' with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Iran's foreign ministry rejected President Trump's accusations the country is developing chemical or biological weapons and compared the situation to then-Secretary of State Colin Powell asserting Iraq had weapons of mass destruction.
"After the grand narrative of the 'Iranian nuclear threat,' U.S. officials are now claiming that there are indications Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons!" Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X . "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar. Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."
Baqaei raised the specter of the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003 over alleged development of weapons of mass destruction by Saddam Hussein's government and asked why Americans would fall for it again.
"Do American officials really expect the world to forget Colin Powell's infamous appearance before the U.N. Security Council in 2003, when he held up a small vial as a visual representation of the alleged threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction?" the spokesperson said. "That moment has since become an enduring symbol of one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history."
He added, "And now we find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script."
Mr. Trump on Wednesday had claimed there was an "indication" Iran was looking to develop chemical or biological weapons because the U.S. had "shut them out" of obtaining nuclear weapons.
"They're looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," Mr. Trump told a Fox reporter in Shenzhen, China.
The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.
In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.
Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.
The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic.
Iraqi forces will begin deploying on Friday in the main stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group, state media reported, as Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi steps up efforts to rein in the faction.
Kataeb Hezbollah on Tuesday adopted a softer tone toward the U.S.-backed premier, with Iraqi sources saying a compromise was reached during a visit by Iranian commander Esmail Qaani.
Iraq has faced mounting U.S. pressure to curb Iran's influence and contain Tehran-backed armed groups — a difficult task in a country long caught between its two allies.
Tensions have grown between Zaidi and Kataeb Hezbollah since the U.S.-backed leader vowed to disarm Iran-backed groups that have long-targeted U.S. interests in the region — a longstanding American demand but a tall order for Baghdad.
This week, Zaidi gave Kataeb Hezbollah a deadline to withdraw from Jurf al-Sakher, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, which lies south of Baghdad, after the government said an investigative committee had confirmed oil smuggling in the area — a claim the armed group denied.
President Trump told Channel 12 News in Israel that he is in no hurry to make any decisions on the war with Iran, and could in fact wait until next year.
"I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran," Mr. Trump told Keshet 12's Barak Ravid, who spoke to the president as he returned from China. "We'll see what happens after the new year starts."
The story noted Mr. Trump could also change his mind, though.
The tone seems in line with his and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments from last week. Mr. Trump called new strikes "quite unlikely," while Rubio said new strikes weren't needed since the economic sanctions campaign was working so well.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he had no need to ask China or Russia for help with an Iran deal.
"They want to make a deal, so I don't need help," Mr. Trump told the network. "I mean, I'm not going to go in asking for help. And frankly, they've treated us very well. They haven't fired. They haven't put ships in the water."
The war against Iran has cost the U.S. military more than $48 billion since the conflict began in late February, a Pentagon official said Thursday.
"That number includes munitions, equipment replacement costs, and operational cost," Arthur Miller, the Pentagon's deputy comptroller, told lawmakers during a hearing on his nomination as assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management.
The figure does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, some of which have been hit hard by Iranian drone and missile attacks, nor does it take into account the harm to the global economy.
The update was the first since mid-October, when the war's cost was pegged at $47.1 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News. The bulk of that price tag at the time was replacing used munitions at about $29 billion. Lost equipment, including planes and unmanned aircraft, accounted for about $6 billion.
Iran said Thursday that it will not accept "unconditional and unlimited cooperation" with inspectors from the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency while it is being bombed.
"We do not accept being targeted on the one hand and being asked in a demanding tone on the other to provide accurate information about our materials and facilities and to provide unlimited access to them," Reza Najafi, Iran's ambassador and permanent representative to the United Nations and international organizations in Vienna, said Thursday, according to Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency.
"While adhering to its obligations, Iran will not accept unconditional and unlimited cooperation with the Agency [IAEA] and will review each inspection request on a case-by-case basis, taking into account security conditions," he added.
The nuclear issue, including IAEA access to Iran's nuclear sites, has been a key sticking point in negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
President Trump has justified the war as a necessary action to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has always denied any nuclear weapons aspirations, but it has enriched uranium to near-weapons grade. The exact whereabouts and condition of that material, and the circumstances of many facilities themselves, have remained unclear since the U.S. and Israel launched a major attack on the sites in June 2025. Iran has refused IAEA access to its nuclear facilities since then.
Saudi Arabia has condemned Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen for targeting a skyscraper in the financial district of Riyadh, the kingdom's capital.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's strong condemnation and denunciation of the continued terrorist attacks by the Houthi terrorist militia targeting civilian and economic facilities and civilian objects in the capital, Riyadh, and the resulting material damage to the King Abdullah Financial District," the ministry wrote in a post on X .
Earlier, Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said the building was damaged in a Houthi strike but that there were no injuries.
The Iran-backed Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district on Thursday, causing damage but no injuries, Saudi authorities said.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin themselves, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes .
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking , a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to the press.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta, in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
It was not immediately clear when the meeting concluded, after roughly an hour and a half, whether the three leaders had reached any substantive understandings. They were expected to discuss arms control and the wars in Iran and Ukraine, among other matters.
An initial readout of the meeting first released by the Russian side listed four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically,  overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against Tehran earlier this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the top of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that he, and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since the two held a summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in Trump’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with both Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering, despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.
Xi greeted Trump at the steps of Air Force One upon his arrival in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening, reciprocating the rare honor Trump extended to the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington in September.
While Trump’s meetings with Xi were the primary purpose of his visit, the Chinese leader is also hosting a major international conference, gathering leaders from around the world for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.

articles.title_orig: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: Costco sees panic buying surge after tech outages, report says

articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major tech outages over the last week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios.
Why it matters: Purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting public anxiety over the outages and fragile infrastructure, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups.
Catch up quick: Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency each faced outages over the last week.
Yes, but: There's no publicly established evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack, despite the theories circulating online.
By the numbers: Suspected bots accounted for roughly 30% of posts promoting conspiracy theories about several recent tech outages, according to data from social media monitoring firm PeakMetrics.
Threat level: Jessica Pratt, a spokesperson for PeakMetrics, told Axios that most of the bot activity is aimed at "gaming the platforms' algorithms" and that it sees some foreign influence within that — although the company could not detail precisely how many of the bots are tied to foreign state media and governments.
Zoom in: The most popular theory being pushed was that each of these incidents must be connected.
The big picture: Foreign influence operations have historically used bots to amplify political grievances and spread false narratives, but it's unclear who's operating the accounts pushing theories about the latest outages.
Between the lines: The longer outages dragged on without clear explanations, the more room conspiracy theories had to spread.
The intrigue: Questions about whether the outages are connected have also reached Washington, where senior officials and lawmakers are raising concerns about what might be causing the disruptions.
What we're watching: Outages are about to become the new normal as organizations race to patch critical vulnerabilities discovered by AI before hackers can use AI to weaponize them.

articles.title_orig: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
articles.title_zh: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
The Commerce Department, AMD and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks continued.
The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including Bytedance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third controls.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.
— Megan Cassella and Daren Fonda contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
articles.title_zh: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
articles.content_orig:
Officials were frank heading into Thursday’s unprecedented three-way talks : US President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin were unlikely to leave Shenzhen with any major agreements.
Diplomatic breakthroughs, it turned out, were not the point. The talks themselves were the deliverable.
Gathered at a round table inside a state guesthouse on the outskirts of this modern metropolis, each man cited the “responsibility” on them to jointly navigate a complicated world.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure; when great powers clash, the world is in chaos,” Xi said as the talks were starting.
Each was also looking to gain something from the power projection the meeting afforded.
For Putin, it was a chance to reemerge on the biggest global platform, with vastly more powerful nations, after being shunned nearly five years ago for his invasion of Ukraine. A joint statement released after the meeting listed immunity for state officials as “of fundamental importance,” a matter of significance for a leader who is wanted for war crimes by the International Criminal Court.
Xi was able to portray himself — and China — as a diplomatic power player, even as economic problems dog him at home.
And Trump, whose lame-duck era was hastened after this month’s midterm election battering, was able to show he’s still in the game with two men whose power in their own countries goes mostly unchecked.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech together,” Trump said as the meeting began. “We are choosing a different course.”
“Let’s see if we can get something done,” he said before the press was dismissed and the meeting got underway.
Here are five takeaways from the summit in Shenzhen.
Whether Thursday’s meeting will be remembered as a historic pivot point — or just another photo-op — isn’t yet clear. Eighty-one minutes was hardly enough time to resolve all the major differences between the three countries, on wars, economics and cutting-edge technology.
Heading into the talks, the leaders’ objectives seemed to differ.
The summit was initially proposed by Putin as a way to discuss the war in Ukraine without representatives from Ukraine at the table — a prospect that sent shivers through Kyiv and led to comparisons to the 1945 Yalta conference, when world powers carved up the postwar world into spheres of influence.
Both Xi and Putin referenced the post-World War II moment in their opening remarks as a time when powerful countries joined together to shape the world, a hint of how they viewed Thursday’s encounter.
Initially, American officials said Ukraine would not be on the agenda — though Trump later said he would bring it up.
“I think things are happening. I think that (Putin) and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war,” he said at the start of the meeting.
Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
More important, in Trump’s mind, was a discussion on nuclear arms control among the world’s largest nuclear states. Trump wants to negotiate a new nonproliferation pact with Moscow and Beijing, though he was candid about the difficulties of reaching an agreement.
“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them,” he said. “It’s the way life works.”
Xi has appeared uninterested in entering a nuclear agreement with two countries whose arsenals of warheads are many times the size of China’s. And he was initially reluctant to host tripartite talks at all that could overshadow his APEC summit, according to US officials.
Speaking in the hours before the sit-down, Trump was asked about the advantages of meeting the two autocrats together.
“They both like Trump,” he said. “Now, what happens after me? That I can’t tell you.”
The competing objectives for the summit didn’t seem to matter once the men arrived at the Kylin Villa, alongside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park.
They convened at a round table, spaced apart equally with Xi in the middle.
“We are really making history,” Trump said proudly. “The three of us have a great deal to discuss.”
The relationships on display are complicated. Trump has worked ardently to cultivate both Xi and Putin over the last two years, hoping deeper personal ties will translate into smoother geopolitics. He’s employed flattery and showy summits to fete and elevate his counterparts.
He called both men “friends” in individual meetings beforehand.
“I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem,” Trump told Xi.
The flattery has yet to yield significant breakthroughs. Trump has complained his relationship with Putin, helped along by a summit in Alaska last year, has so far failed to end the Ukraine war . Disputes over trade and shipments of rare earths continue to act as irritants in the US-China relationship. And both countries are providing assistance and technology to Iran.
Xi and Putin, who proclaimed five years ago they were partners “without limits,” have met dozens of times. After another meeting here on Wednesday, Chinese state media declared the relationship was “steadfast as a rock through wind and rain.”
Xi and Putin have long been united by a shared view that the global balance of power is undergoing a fundamental shift in their favor, as the East rises and the West is in decline. Or, said another way, that the age of the American superpower is ending.
With this unprecedented three-way meeting with Trump, Xi and Putin have clinched what both are sure to use as a new, landmark testament to that view.
Two of the three men in Thursday’s meeting are embroiled in wars against smaller adversaries that have stretched on longer than anticipated. Trump’s war in Iran and Putin’s war in Ukraine have each sapped military resources and led to global price increases — and frustrated Xi, who sees the conflicts as a threat to global stability.
Both wars were topics Trump hoped to discuss with Xi and Putin, each of whom maintains ties with Tehran. Trump has not applied pressure on Moscow or Beijing to cut off their ties. In fact, he loosened sanctions on Russian diesel , applied after the invasion of Ukraine, in an attempt to bring down costs that spiked as a result of the Iran war, indirectly allowing that conflict to enrich Russia.
Trump has grown exasperated by all the war. The conflict in Iran, which he initially said would last six weeks, is highly unpopular at home and, by his own admission, led to sweeping Republican losses in the midterms. He is now weighing military options to restart a new, intensive round of bombing.
Meanwhile, his campaign pledge to resolve the Ukraine war within 24 hours of taking office is now 667 days overdue.
How much help Xi and Putin will be in ending the wars isn’t clear. And how much a summit without Ukraine or Iran at the table can do toward bringing peace seems limited.
Still, Trump appeared hopeful.
“A lot of people weren’t sure would something come out of it. I think something … will come out,” Trump said beforehand as he met with Xi. “I mean, very very strongly. I think something will come out.”
Over in Berlin, Jared Kushner said that Trump dialed into the meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” and gave his assessment of the talks in Shenzhen.
The president’s son-in-law — speaking alongside the leaders of Germany, France, Ukraine and the United Kingdom at the summit — said Trump had conveyed “a very strong message to both of them [Xi and Putin] on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
He didn’t elaborate but said Trump “came away believing that peace is achievable.”
Steve Witkoff, the president’s special envoy, said that Trump had made “Ukraine and a peaceful end to this” a central part of his message in Shenzhen.

articles.title_orig: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
articles.title_zh: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
articles.content_orig:
2:34 PM EST on November 19, 2026
The first time I played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was during a hurricane. It was late 1999, I was 10 years old, Hurricane Irene was bearing down on Miami, and my friend Ryan had come over to spend the night. He had brought his copy of Ocarina of Time , the game a year old at that point, and his plan was that we should play it all the way to the end. This was a bold goal for two idiot preteen boys, and though we plowed through the entire Child Link part of the game and the start of Adult Link's quest to release the temple sages, the Water Temple claimed us as its own. We didn't have a Prima strategy guide or the internet to help us out, so after hours (and I do mean hours) of raising and lowering water levels, we gave up. I didn't end up beating my own copy of Ocarina of Time , which my dad bought for me as soon as the hurricane passed, until the next summer in Venezuela, but even then, even as an idiot preteen boy, I knew I had played something special.
Twenty-seven years later, I am playing something special again. Well, I am playing the same thing again, but newer, fresher, and more beautiful. I am playing the remake of Ocarina of Time , and I have loved every second of it so far. As a remake, this is a work of art. The graphics are gorgeous, if a bit shiny. The story is as good as it ever was, only now with a lot more voice acting that gives characters personality. The gameplay is much the same, albeit with some quality-of-life changes; the ability to swap equipped items with one button is a huge upgrade to pausing and going into the menu every three seconds. I'm not saying that the remake is now the best way to play Ocarina of Time —there's something to be said for the friction that came with the original's technical limitations—but I am saying that the remake justifies its own existence with an attention to detail and a commitment to thrilling gameplay that shines through in every second of playtime.
In my time with the remake, I have learned to love the quirks and anxieties of a game that is rightfully considered among the very best to ever exist. I have also remembered that when Ocarina of Time gets something right, there's nothing like it. The puzzles are never too confusing, but they have a tactile pacing that makes every step towards the solution feel like a victory. The way the game teaches you to play it is unrivaled. It all fits like a perfect jigsaw, never throwing too much at the player while still challenging them to think creatively. I'm not one for adventure games in this vein anymore, which is probably why I have only played a few Zelda games since Ocarina and its sequel, but every time I opened a previously locked door, I had the forbidden thought of, "Should I play the whole Zelda series now?" There's no higher praise from me than saying Ocarina has me wondering if I should play Skyward Sword .
Ocarina of Time isn't the only blast from the past I've played recently. I have played World of Warcraft off and mostly on since early 2005, and I have tried every variation that the game has had to offer over that time. There is what people call "retail," which is the default game that has progressed from its messy origins to now, 11 expansions later. Retail these days feels like a completely different game than what I started playing, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. In 2019, Blizzard, the game's developers, caved to massive player pressure and released World of Warcraft Classic , essentially launching the game again from scratch, but with some changes to make it a bit more modern.
Classic was a big success, and has continued on since then. As the years of Classic went on, however, players wanted more. They wanted what was deemed " Classic Plus ," essentially the old game but with more twists and turns and new gameplay additions. Blizzard listened with Season of Discovery in 2023. This mode added a lot of abilities from later WoW as well as some new roles for long-time classes. For example, mages could now be healers and shamans could be grossly overpowered tanks. SoD was an even bigger success than Classic , all things considered, because it showed that the skeleton of WoW could support a new evolution.
That brings us to World of Warcraft: Forever , the new game mode that launched on Nov. 4 to record-breaking numbers. It seems that anyone and everyone who had ever played some form of WoW dipped into Forever to check it out. What is it, though? Forever is what Blizzard intends to be a different evolution of Classic . Classes got new tools and toys to play with, but they are not as wild as in SoD . Instead, Blizzard made everyone a bit stronger, a bit more fun to play, but still very much in the realm of old-school gameplay. The innovations instead seem to be coming from the new things players can do. Forever has added new zones in the open world, new dungeons to explore, and starting next month, new raids for groups of 10, 20, or 40 people.
In other words, Forever is an alternate timeline in which Blizzard decided to never release expansion packs, and instead keep everyone's max level at 60 and progress them horizontally. This allows the developers the ability to explore parts of the original world that were under-served, and turn them into new adventures with that Classic vibe. Forever is a much cozier game than what Retail WoW has become, much slower in its gameplay and progression. As the name implies, there is no rush here; this is meant to last as long as players keep logging in, and that makes everything feel more meaningful. The new weapon you got, or the new piece of armor, or a fancy trinket that gives you special powers ... all of those things are meant to, in some way or another, last for the duration of your character's lifespan, rather than getting replaced every four months with a new season.
I have not quit Retail WoW , but I fully took a break to dive into Forever when it released. In the two weeks since, I have played an obscene amount— Forever added viable controller support, so I've been playing on my laptop on the couch while watching TV—and have gotten my first character, a shaman, to level 60. It took me four days, 20 hours, and 29 minutes played to do so. Forever has taken over. Add in the roughly 12 hours of Ocarina of Time that have gotten me to the precipice of the Water Temple, and I've been living in video game past almost exclusively this month.
Though I've enjoyed wrapping myself in the warmth of nostalgia, what I've found most satisfying about this extended foray into the past is the usefulness of my familiarity. I'd consider myself an expert on leveling up characters in every version of WoW Classic at this point, so I was able to lock in and move my way from level 1 to 60 faster than anyone else I know. In Ocarina , my memories from two decades ago, as well as years of watching "BEST ZELDA DUNGEONS RANKED" YouTube videos, have come back to me and I am breezing through the game at a speed that would have befuddled my younger self. The Forest Temple is clearly the best dungeon in the game, and maybe in all of Zelda , but I steamrolled through all of the twisty hallways, tricky Poe mini-bosses, and the Phantom Ganon boss fight. As a child, that fight took me ages.
The ease with which these games have come back to me could have been a letdown, but I'm having a blast. My instincts are better, my stick skills have improved, and my reflexes, though worse than they were say in my early 20s, are more honed from so many hours of games. What these two excursions into my own gaming past have taught me is that I have really been on a journey of self-improvement—I see know lame that sounds—and the sense of accomplishment I get now is not from finishing something, but from finishing it in style.
It's interesting to me that I pregamed Grand Theft Auto VI , perhaps the most technologically advanced game of all time, with two dips into a simpler past. I don't know if I did i

articles.title_orig: What the Blue Wave in Texas Means for Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX
articles.title_zh: What the Blue Wave in Texas Means for Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX
articles.content_orig:
On Valentine’s Day in 2024, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott interrupted a private dinner with his wife to take a call from Elon Musk.
Mr. Musk had recently been rebuked by a court in Delaware, where his two largest companies, SpaceX and Tesla, were incorporated. A judge had voided Mr. Musk’s pay package at Tesla, valued at about $50 billion, calling it “an unfathomable sum.”
Mr. Musk had spent years building a close relationship with the Republican governor. Now, on the call, Mr. Musk wanted to know if Mr. Abbott would support Mr. Musk’s businesses if he incorporated them in Texas, rather than Delaware.
“One hundred percent,” Mr. Abbott said, recounting the story in a 2025 speech at the University of Texas School of Law.
Mr. Musk followed through, further entwining his trillion-dollar electric vehicle maker, Tesla, and his two-trillion-dollar rocket maker, SpaceX, with the state. Mr. Musk had been cultivating Texas’s Republican leaders since he moved there in 2020. For a while, the strategy paid off handsomely. Mr. Abbott held up his end of the Valentine’s Day bargain, awarding Mr. Musk and his businesses at least $1.7 billion in grants, tax breaks and other incentives in the past two years, according to a New York Times analysis.
Since this month’s election , Mr. Musk’s big bet on Texas has become vulnerable. Texans voted out many of his political allies, including Mr. Abbott , even after Mr. Musk gave Republicans nearly $500 million nationwide.

"GTA 6" is no different — but this time, Silicon Valley is the butt of the joke.
The new game, which launched on Thursday, is full of techie doppelgängers: delivery services, ride-hailing apps, and social platforms that look familiar, but now have overtly sexual names.

articles.title_orig: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
articles.title_zh: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on third-party vendors
articles.title_zh: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on third-party vendors
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Visa ( V ), and Mastercard ( MA ) said on Thursday that some select customer data, including names and emails, was accessed by attackers after a cyberattack on a vendor.
Spokespeople for the companies said no payments or card data was leaked and that their own systems were not affected by the incident.
JPMorgan said it believes hackers who attacked a third-party vendor accessed marketing data, including customer names and email addresses. The bank also said the incident isn't related to outages many of its customers reported earlier this week, which it blamed on a software bug .
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said.
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," a Mastercard spokesperson said. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the person added.
A Visa spokesperson added claims of the incident are associated to a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region.
"This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week," the Visa spokesperson added.
A ransomware group known as n0n has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the dark web and shared sample data as proof, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar.
The cybersecurity firm told Yahoo Finance that it hasn't independently verified whether the ransomware group carried out the intrusion. It also supported JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard's statements that the breaches most likely originated at a third-party vendor and involved marketing and benefit-program data such as names and email addresses.
"The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," SOCRadar chief information security officer Ensar Seker said in an emailed statement.
The latest incident comes as consumers are on high alert after a string of major technology outages this November . The Wall Street Journal earlier reported the connection between the breaches and the ransomware group.

articles.title_orig: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.title_zh: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
AMD ( AMD ) stock plunged more than 8% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media published an investigation raising questions about potential export-control issues related to the chipmaker's products.
Hunterbrook Media is associated with Hunterbrook Capital, which has a short position on AMD.
According to the outlet , Chinese server maker IEIT continued to receive firmware updates for AMD's chips, despite being blacklisted by the US Department of Commerce.
Hunterbrook also claims three companies associated with IEIT, but not blacklisted, used software virtually identical to the firmware used by IEIT.
AMD, however, refuted Hunterbrook's claims in a statement to Yahoo Finance.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," a company spokesperson wrote.
"AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
AMD rival Nvidia ( NVDA ) has also faced scrutiny over former CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy and over concerns that customers circumvented export controls by shipping chips to China.
Huang resigned from Nvidia late last week and was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress.
AMD is viewed as a potential beneficiary of Nvidia's stumbles.
The company's stock is up more than 110% over the past 12 months, while Nvidia shares are down as much as 18%.
The AI trade has faced a number of headwinds recently as investors question the stability of the AI build-out and whether the boom will continue at its current pace.
